\section[l'infermiera]{l'infermiera — a nurse}

\label{lesson:IT-C111-infermiera}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for a walnut, then the Italian for pepper.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: l'infermiera}
\textbf{l'infermiera} — \textquotedblleft{}a nurse\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{infermiera} — built from the old word \emph{infermo}, \textquotedblleft{}sick\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{-iera}, the ending for a woman who does a job: the woman who tends the sick. \emph{infermo} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{infirmus}, \textquotedblleft{}not strong, weak\textquotedblright{} — inherited. (EtymDB 2.1)
\end{cousinweb}

\section[il contadino]{il contadino — a farmer}

\label{lesson:IT-C111-contadino}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for a police officer, then the Italian for a shop assistant.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: il contadino}
\textbf{il contadino} — \textquotedblleft{}a farmer\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{contadino} — built from \emph{contado}, the farmland around a city, with \emph{-ino}, \textquotedblleft{}one who belongs to it\textquotedblright{}. \emph{contado} goes back to Latin \emph{comitatus}, the lands of a count. EtymDB 2.1 records the Latin word but not the Italian steps.
\end{cousinweb}
